title: Where it held on
hookLine: in Nepal's Newar communities, the Himalayas and the hills of Bengal, the practice continued

cards: In the Kathmandu Valley, in the courtyard of an old monastery, a man in ordinary clothes opens a manuscript in Sanskrit and begins a ritual. He is a Vajracharya, a priest of Newar Buddhism.
He may be married, with children, and tradition says the role passes down through families. No lifelong robes, no monastery to sleep in, just a household and a family calling.
And yet the texts he honors come from the same world as the great monasteries of India.

teach.b: The Newar people of the Kathmandu Valley kept a form of Buddhism that grew from the same Sanskrit tradition as the Indian monasteries.
Its priests, the Vajracharyas, and householder families called Shakyas live around courtyards that still carry the old name vihara, monastery.

Newar Buddhists keep Sanskrit texts, like the Perfection of Wisdom, and honor them in worship. When scholars went looking for Sanskrit Buddhist works lost in India, some of the manuscripts turned up in Nepal.

Higher in the mountains, in places like Ladakh and Sikkim and the high valleys of Nepal, the practice continued in the forms that had traveled to Tibet: monasteries on ridges, prayer flags, chanting in Tibetan.

Third, the hills of Bengal. In the far east of the old Bengal region, communities such as the Barua and the Chakma kept Buddhist practice alive in their villages, with monks and festivals of their own.
Fourth, what that changes. The story of Buddhism in India is often told with an ending. These communities complicate it.
Small, often far from the cities, sometimes under pressure, they kept going: a family priesthood, a mountain monastery, a village temple with a few monks.
Nothing dramatic. Just the same rituals, done again next week, and the week after.

how: Newar Buddhists in the Kathmandu Valley gather in courtyard monasteries for rituals led by Vajracharya priests, and Buddhist communities in the Himalayas and the hills of Bangladesh and eastern India keep their own temples and festivals.

On each out-breath, honor the people who show up when it would be easier not to.
